property_summary: When owner is called, the returned address must be non-zero after construction, but the bug returns address(0), breaking that invariant.
For any caller, c.owner() must equal the address that was set as owner during construction (which is non-zero), but the buggy version returns address(0) for every caller, violating this equality.
The owner() return value must equal the deployer address (address(this)) set in setUp(), but the mutant returns address(0) for all callers.

For any call to owner() by any address, the returned address must be the same as the immutable owner stored during construction, and querying it a second time must return the same address as the first call; the bug returns address(0) on every call, so the two responses differ.
After construction, calling c.owner() should return the same non-zero address as the deployer (address(this)), but the mutant returns address(0).

The owner() function must always return the address that was set as the owner during contract construction or via transferOwnership; the bug returns msg.sender, so any caller other than the original owner will see a different address.

The owner() function returns the same address for any caller as long as ownership hasn’t been explicitly transferred, but the bug makes it return msg.sender, so two different callers see different owner addresses.
c.owner() returns the same address regardless of the caller if ownership has not changed, but the bug makes it return msg.sender, so two different callers will see different return values.

For any two callers, c.owner() returns identical values as long as ownership hasn't been transferred, but the buggy version returns msg.sender causing different callers to see different owner addresses.

c.owner() returns the same address for any caller as long as ownership hasn't been explicitly transferred, but the bug makes it return msg.sender, so two different callers will see different return values.

The `owner()` function always returns the address that was originally set as owner during deployment; the bug makes it return the contract's own address instead, so calling `transferOwnership` with a new owner address will change the stored owner in the correct contract but not in the buggy one, and subsequent `owner()` calls will reveal the difference.
The owner() return value must equal the address passed as newOwner in a preceding transferOwnership call; the bug makes owner() return address(this) instead of the passed argument.

After deployment, c.owner() must equal the owner set during construction (the first argument to the constructor); the mutant returns address(c) instead, so c.owner() != address(this) for any non-self-deployer.
For any address callable by the owner, after transferOwnership(newOwner), owner() must return newOwner; the bug makes it return address(this) instead.

For any authorized caller, after owner() returns address X, a subsequent transferOwnership(X) as owner must not cause owner() to change to a different value; the bug makes owner() always return address(this), which breaks this invariant when address(this) differs from the stored owner and a legit ownership transfer is attempted.
Ownership can never be transferred to the zero address in the reference contract, but the buggy version allows the zero address to become the owner.
After any call to transferOwnership, the owner() must not be address(0) for the reference, but the bug allows owner() to become address(0) after transferOwnership(address(0)).

For any input newOwner, if transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds in a single top-level call, then immediately after owner() must equal newOwner. The buggy version allows transferring to a zero-address newOwner where the call succeeds (does not revert) yet the subsequent owner() is zero, violating this invariant because the reference version never changes owner to zero on a non-reverting call to transferOwnership.

For any call to transferOwnership(newOwner) that does not revert, owner() must equal newOwner afterwards; the buggy version allows a non-reverting call with newOwner = address(0) yet owner() remains the previous owner, violating this rule.

For any successful (non-reverting) call to transferOwnership(newOwner), the newOwner must not be the zero address; the buggy version removes this check, allowing transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed and set the zero address as owner.
After setOperator is called by the owner with any argument, operator must equal the argument; the bug sets it to msg.sender instead.

After a non-owner address calls setOperator (which should revert), the operator variable must remain unchanged; the buggy version sets operator to msg.sender regardless of caller, allowing a non-owner to become operator.
After a successful call to setOperator by the owner, the operator variable must equal the _operator argument; the buggy version sets it to msg.sender regardless of the argument.
After the owner calls setOperator, the operator must equal the address passed as argument; the buggy version ignores the argument and sets operator to the owner's address (msg.sender).
After the owner calls setOperator(a) where a != owner(), the operator must equal a; the bug sets it to the owner (msg.sender) instead.

After any successful call to setOperator, the operator state variable must equal the address argument passed to it; the buggy version never updates operator, so after a first call any subsequent call with a different _operator leaves operator unchanged, violating the rule.
After a call to setOperator by the owner with any address a, operator() must equal a, but the buggy version never updates operator, so operator() stays unchanged from its initial value.

After a call to setOperator by the owner, the operator() getter must return the _operator argument; the buggy version never updates operator, so operator() remains the initial value from construction.
After any call to setOperator by the owner, the operator must equal the argument, but the buggy version ignores the argument so operator retains the prior value.

After any two calls to setOperator by the owner with different arguments, the operator() returned after the second call must differ from the operator() returned after the first call; the buggy version never updates operator, so both calls return the identical initial value.
Only the owner can change the operator; the buggy version allows anyone to set the operator, violating exclusive ownership control.
After any call to setOperator, the previous operator remains unchanged unless the caller is the owner; the buggy version allows a non-owner to change it, breaking this invariant.
For any caller, the operator should change only if the caller is the original owner; the buggy version allows any caller to change it, violating owner-exclusive operator mutation.
For any caller, the operator can be changed only by the owner; the buggy version allows any caller, including a non-owner, to change it, violating exclusive owner control.
Except the initial owner, no one can change the operator; the buggy version removes the onlyOwner modifier, allowing any caller to set the operator, breaking this exclusivity.

After any successful call to setRewardsRecipient, the public getter rewardsRecipient() must return the address passed as argument; the buggy version leaves it unchanged, so a subsequent getReward call that relies on rewardsRecipient can misdirect rewards.
After a successful call to setRewardsRecipient, rewardsRecipient() must return the address passed as the argument.
